report.source_text: On the examination, there were bilateral cranial neuropathies involving trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves. Lateral gaze was restricted bilaterally and there was bilateral upper and lower facial weakness with impaired eyebrow raise, eye closure and inability to smile. Weber’s test lateralised to the left ear and Rinne’s test demonstrated air conduction greater than bone bilaterally. Tongue was weak but midline on protrusion. Sensation was decreased to light touch and pinprick in V2 distribution on the right side. The remained of the neurological examination was unremarkable.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Early syphilitic meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 37-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive neurological complaints including disequilibrium, unsteadiness, difficulty closing eyes, right lip numbness, bilateral hearing impairment, and slurred speech. Neurological examination revealed bilateral cranial neuropathies involving trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII), and hypoglossal (XII) nerves. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed elevated protein and lymphocyte predominant leucocytosis, consistent with meningitis. MRI of the brain with gadolinium demonstrated enhancement of the trigeminal, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves. Serum serology confirmed active syphilis infection with positive TPPA, CMIA IgG/IgM, and an RPR titre of 1:32. These findings collectively supported the diagnosis of early syphilitic meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with progressive neurological complaints including disequilibrium, unsteadiness, difficulty closing eyes, right lip numbness, bilateral hearing impairment and slurred speech.

Neurological examination revealed bilateral cranial neuropathies involving trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves, with restricted lateral gaze, bilateral upper and lower facial weakness, and decreased sensation in V2 distribution on the right side.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination demonstrated elevated protein (1.28 g/L) and lymphocyte predominant leucocytosis (0.441x10^9/L), consistent with meningitis.
MRI of the brain with gadolinium demonstrated enhancement of the trigeminal nerve at the pons, as well as facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at the geniculate ganglion.

Serum T. pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA) and chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) IgG and IgM were positive, with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titre of 1:32, consistent with active syphilis infection.
